case_study_insert.main_stem: Merrivale Boutiques (MVB) is a retail cooperative in the fashion boutique and omnichannel retail sector, employing a workforce of 78. Founded in 2005 by Priya Raval, the business runs member-owned fashion boutiques and a click-and-collect website and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership. MVB plans to invest $480,000 in a new click-and-collect store network and website upgrade, financed by a $300,000 bank loan and $180,000 member share issue. It has fixed costs of $120,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.00 a unit and a selling price of $10.00, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. MVB faces two operational problems: stockouts affected 7.8% of listed fashion lines and customer complaints about service have risen.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Retail Operations Report â€” Q3 2025: The boutique chain and website sold 19,200 units, with stockouts on 7.8% of listed lines and fabric waste of 5.1% of material used. Customer complaints rose from 31 to 44 per month. Average click-and-collect readiness time is 2.6 days. A survey of 700 shoppers found that 63% would pay up to $0.45 more for a reliable click-and-collect service, and 55% prefer retailers with clear sustainability policies. A training audit shows 16 of 78 store staff have not completed customer-service induction; a workshop costs $95 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.00% to 5.75%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.60 to $13.50 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills across retail and warehousing. (3) Wholesale fashion garment costs have risen 10.2% year-on-year, consumer spending in boutique retail grew 2.2%, and inflation is running at 6.8%.

questions.question_text: MVB plans to fund part of its $480,000 expansion with a $300,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for MVB of using $180,000 member share capital instead.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A member share capital issue raises $180,000 without interest charges or a fixed repayment date, unlike the $300,000 bank loan that would commit MVB to regular servicing. Equity finance makes the $480,000 click-and-collect expansion more resilient if consumer spending in boutique retail grows only 2.2% as Appendix 3 forecasts.

Point 2: Because MVB is a retail cooperative, share capital from its own members deepens member loyalty and commitment to the a new click-and-collect store network and website upgrade, aligning finance with the 78 staff and member-customers. No lender can repossess assets if trading slips, and the cooperative keeps control of its democratic decisions. The loan alternative would create debt service that could force cutbacks in member service and the fashion boutique and omnichannel retail offering.

Taken together, the $180,000 funds a new click-and-collect store network and website upgrade without competing with the $300,000 debt service, leaving the $120,000 of annual fixed costs to be covered by the $4.00 contribution on each of the 70,000 units. In fashion boutique and omnichannel retail, where the 10.2% input-cost rise already pressures margins, avoiding compulsory interest payments gives MVB a materially safer route than increasing its borrowings for a hierarchical organisation with 78 staff.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to Merrivale Boutiques and its financing choice.

questions.question_text: MVB is promoting its fashion boutique and omnichannel retail offering. Consider in-store leaflets, social media advertising, or loyalty-card email marketing. Which should MVB choose to promote its click-and-collect service? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
In-store leaflets: Leaflets distributed in the boutiques are cheap and give existing member-customers details of the new click-and-collect service, but they reach only people already in store and generate little measurable response for a fashion boutique and omnichannel retail cooperative trying to grow online.

Social media advertising: Paid social campaigns can target fashion shoppers broadly and drive traffic to the website, building awareness of the 480,000 service. Costs can escalate and the audience is not always local to the boutiques, so some spend is wasted.

Loyalty-card email marketing: Emails to the cooperative's existing members are low-cost, measurable and go to known customers who already trust the brand, matching the 55%% of surveyed shoppers who prefer clear sustainability policies. The reach is limited to the existing database, so it will not attract many new members on its own.

Recommendation: MVB should choose loyalty-card email marketing. It reaches known, trusting member-customers at almost no extra cost and can promote the click-and-collect service directly, which fits a cooperative with 78 staff. In-store leaflets are rejected as too narrow and hard to measure, and broad social media is rejected as costly and poorly targeted at existing members compared with email.

With fixed costs of $120,000 a year and a $300,000 loan to service, MVB needs volume at a controlled cost, so the chosen method must reach buyers who will actually convert; that is why the two rejected options, despite their superficial appeal, are set aside in favour of the more targeted approach. The decision should be reviewed against the sales and enquiry figures in Appendix 1 after one campaign cycle, and the spend justified only if the extra orders cover the $4.00 contribution needed toward the $120,000 fixed costs of the fashion boutique and omnichannel retail business.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of promotional methods with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of the business with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of Merrivale Boutiques with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the two rejected options lose.

questions.question_text: MVB's stockouts and rising complaints are hurting member service. Explain two benefits for MVB of using democratic leadership in its stores.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the 78 store staff voice ideas on preventing the stockouts affecting 7.8% of lines, drawing on their direct customer contact. This suits a retail cooperative where member-customers and employees expect a say, and the resulting commitment can help reverse the rise in complaints from 31 to 44 a month.

Point 2: Consulting staff before the click-and-collect expansion builds support for new working practices and improves service quality, protecting the fashion boutique and omnichannel retail offering. With a hierarchical structure, Priya Raval can still make final decisions, but involvement raises motivation and retention, which matters when the $480,000 website and store network must be staffed reliably.

These benefits matter because fixed costs of $120,000 mean MVB must keep output close to 70,000 units a year; every experienced worker lost through turnover or absence is replaced at a retraining cost shown in Appendix 1, and a destabilised team would slow the $480,000 rollout. Better motivation therefore protects the quality figures reported in Appendix 1 and the $4.00 contribution on each unit, which is what allows the retail cooperative to absorb the 10.2% rise in fashion garment costs without cutting the 70,000-unit plan.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to Merrivale Boutiques's problem, costs and output.

questions.question_text: MVB must train staff to use its new equipment. Consider on-the-job customer-service induction or an external workshop at $95 per employee. Which should MVB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job customer-service induction: Coaching in the boutiques is specific to MVB's service standards and member expectations, costs no external fee, and keeps the 16 staff selling while they learn, which helps tackle the stockouts on 7.8% of lines and the rise in complaints to 44. Trainers are busy staff and recorded certification is weak for a cooperative expanding its $480,000 network.

External workshop at $95 per employee: A structured workshop gives consistent service skills and a completion record for all 16 staff, costing 16 Ã— $95 = $1,520, small against the $480,000 investment. It takes staff away from the shops and may be generic, so on-site reinforcement would be needed.

Decision: MVB should choose on-the-job customer-service induction, followed by a short workshop for team leaders. It is cheaper, tailored to member service and avoids losing selling hours; the full workshop programme is rejected because removing 16 staff and paying $1,520 would disrupt the click-and-collect launch.

The wider context reinforces this decision. With fixed costs of $120,000 and the $300,000 loan to service, MVB cannot afford the output loss that follows withdrawing the staff concerned from the line for long. The documented problem in Appendix 1 â€” the defect and turnover figures â€” makes early practical competence on the actual equipment more valuable than a generic certificate. A short external top-up later can add formal recognition without the disruption of full off-the-job training, so the chosen blend protects both the 70,000-unit volume and the quality the retail cooperative is trying to improve as it invests $480,000 in new fashion boutique and omnichannel retail capacity.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to the business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of the business.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of Merrivale Boutiques with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MVB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs Ã· Contribution per unit. Substitution: $120,000 Ã· ($10.00 âˆ’ $6.00) = $120,000 Ã· $4.00 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price âˆ’ Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $10.00 âˆ’ $6.00 = $4.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MVB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 70,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 40,000 units, to judge whether the $480,000 investment is safely profitable.
2. Contribution per unit of $4.00 lets managers model a discount: for example a 5% cut in the $10.00 selling price would lower contribution and show the extra volume needed to cover $120,000 fixed costs.
3. With $120,000 fixed costs and $4.00 contribution, managers can set the sales volumes needed to service the $300,000 loan before committing further capital to a new click-and-collect store network and website upgrade.
4. Unit cost of about $7.71 ($120,000 Ã· 70,000 units + $6.00) can be benchmarked each quarter to spot waste from the fashion garment cost inflation of 10.2% and to check whether the $6.00 variable cost can be renegotiated. Together these figures guide pricing, volume and cost control at MVB.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 40,000 units against 70,000 output; pricing/discount modelling against $120,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume for the $480,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at about $7.71 to tackle 10.2% input-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MVB's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MVB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.29 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.36 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.70 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $110 inventories + $42 trade receivables + $28 cash = $180; 2025 current assets = $88 + $56 + $36 = $180. Dividing by current liabilities of $140 (2024) and $132 (2025) gives the 2024 figure of 1.29 and the 2025 figure of 1.36. For the second measure, (current assets âˆ’ inventories) Ã· current liabilities gives 2024: ($180 âˆ’ $110) Ã· $140 = $70 Ã· $140 = 0.50; 2025: ($180 âˆ’ $88) Ã· $132 = $92 Ã· $132 = 0.70.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. The 2024 coverage of 1.29 rose to 1.36 in 2025, meaning current assets cover short-term obligations more comfortably, helped by current liabilities falling from $140 to $132. The stricter measure, which excludes inventories, improved from 0.50 to 0.70, so MVB is less dependent on selling stock to meet debts â€” important while it services a $300,000 loan and funds a $480,000 expansion. Trade receivables moved from $42 to $56, tying up cash that could be slower to collect, and inventories moved from $110 to $88, so availability for peak demand should still be watched. Non-current assets grew from $900 to $1,150, consistent with the new investment, while capital employed rose from $1,050 to $1,280.

Conclusion: MVB's financial position has improved. Both short-term solvency measures rose (1.29 to 1.36 and 0.50 to 0.70) and the improvement does not rely on inventory alone. The main residual risk is the $56 of trade receivables, so tighter credit control is advisable before further expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether Merrivale Boutiques's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MVB of introducing a reliable click-and-collect service priced $0.45 higher.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A reliable click-and-collect service at $55% more matches the 63% of surveyed shoppers who would pay for it and the 10.2%% who prefer clear sustainability policies, boosting member loyalty and sales for the $480,000 network.

Disadvantage: Running click-and-collect adds staffing and handling cost that could raise the $6.00 variable cost, squeezing the $4 contribution. Stockouts on 7.8% of lines could undermine the promise if availability is not fixed first.

Managers should set the premium against the $4.00 contribution per unit and the $120,000 annual fixed costs: the survey evidence in Appendix 1 suggests customers will pay more, but the 10.2% rise in fashion garment costs and the need to sustain 70,000 units mean the net gain must be checked. If volumes fall, the extra cost would not be recovered, so the effect should be reviewed after one quarter. For a retail cooperative with 78 staff, the change also affects training and the brand Priya Raval has built, so it belongs alongside the service and quality improvements already reported in Appendix 1 rather than being introduced in isolation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to Merrivale Boutiques's data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.75%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in fashion garment input costs will affect MVB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.00% to 5.75%): The insert states MVB has a $300,000 bank loan. A rise of 0.75 percentage points adds 0.75% Ã— $300,000 = $2,250 a year if the loan is variable-rate; if the rate is fixed, the direct effect is nil. Higher base rates could also raise the cost of future borrowing for the $480,000 expansion and make consumers more cautious about fashion boutique and omnichannel retail spending.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $13.50 per hour): With a workforce of 78, this raises wage costs in the partly hourly-paid fulfilment and store roles. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so no defensible annual wage bill can be invented. The only honest yardstick is the productivity already derivable: 70,000 units Ã· 78 staff = 897 units per worker. A wage rise is absorbable only if productivity holds near that level or output grows, otherwise unit labour costs rise and the $4.00 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (10.2% in fashion garment): MVB's variable cost is $6.00 a unit and the insert does not decompose it, so the only defensible bound is to apply the full rise: 10.2% Ã— $6.00 = $0.612 a unit, which at 70,000 units is about $42,840 a year (70,000 Ã— $0.612). Even a smaller effect would cut the $4.00 contribution and threaten the $480,000 investment; the $55% premium from the survey can recover only part of it.

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in fashion garment costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 70,000 units sold, directly erodes the $4.00 contribution that justifies the $480,000 expansion, and is only partly offset by the premium. The interest rise is smaller ($2,250 at most, and possibly nil), and the wage impact, though unavoidable, can be managed through the 897-unit productivity the business already achieves.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to the business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of Merrivale Boutiques with a well-justified judgment on which has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
